description: We are a dedicated group of students interested in programming, astronomy and learning.
summary:
AstroTwin is a browser-based tool for exploring how spaceflight can affect the human body and how different routines change modeled outcomes. We connect published NASA research with interactive 2D and 3D anatomy, mission timelines and side-by-side routine comparisons.

Users create a flight, select a crew profile and enter available baseline measurements. They can explore changes in hip and spine bone density, leg lean tissue and aerobic fitness from launch through recovery. A routine search evaluates exercise and nutrition options within a chosen time budget, while manual controls let users test alternatives.

The project's research foundation includes published measurements from the 17-person standard-exercise group in the NASA Sprint Study. An interactive research view connects those measurements to the body regions they describe.

AstroTwin makes space-health research easier to investigate by turning published findings into a working visual tool for asking questions, comparing scenarios and understanding trade-offs.
details:
AstroTwin is a working web application that lets users investigate how a space mission could affect the body and compare different ways of responding. It brings crew profiles, mission planning, body visualization and published research into one workspace. Our aim is to make space-health data useful to someone exploring a concrete question, such as how changing the balance between strength training and cardio affects the model's projected condition at landing.

The project starts with NASA research. We use published group measurements from English et al.'s NASA Sprint Study, including the standard-exercise group of 17 astronauts. The model's descriptive calibration uses preflight and postflight hip bone density, lumbar spine bone density, leg lean tissue and aerobic fitness measurements. The research page displays the original measurement units, reported standard errors and testing windows, with direct access to the paper. Measured study results remain distinguishable from the forecasts produced for a user's scenario. NASA Sprint Study

A user begins by creating a flight and assigning a crew profile. They choose a destination and duration, then enter or adjust available baseline measurements. A visual destination selector and editable mission presets make setup quick. Separate saved flights let users revisit scenarios without losing their inputs. The current destination choices are the ISS, Moon and Mars, with shared ISS-based physiological parameters across those scenarios.

The body view provides both an interactive 2D anatomy illustration and a rotatable 3D reference model. Selecting a region connects the anatomy to its relevant measurements. A timeline follows launch, the mission, landing and recovery, while charts show how modeled values change over time. Measurements appear in meaningful units, including g/cm² for bone density and mL/kg/min for aerobic fitness. Optional injury scenarios add an onset day, location and severity so users can explore their assumed effects within the same mission.

Routine comparison is a central feature. Users can choose an objective and daily exercise budget, then let the application evaluate a bounded set of strength, cardio and nutrition combinations through the forecast API. The search returns the best evaluated option for those settings. The recommended routine stays separate from manual edits, so moving a slider does not redefine the recommendation. Users can compare the applied routine with a test routine, inspect the changes at landing and choose whether to apply the alternative. Medication is an explicit scenario setting rather than an automatically selected treatment.

Our design uses the body and mission timeline as navigation. Instead of asking users to interpret a large table before they can explore, the interface lets them select an anatomical region, move through time and compare outcomes visually. The research view follows the same approach, connecting a measurement to the part of the body it describes. This makes it easier to see how the published evidence, model assumptions and displayed results relate to one another.

We built the frontend with React and TypeScript, using Three.js and React Three Fiber for the 3D anatomy, Recharts for graphs and Framer Motion for interface transitions. A Python and FastAPI backend runs the forecast model and serves consistent results to the charts, body views and routine search. Research values and model parameters are stored in inspectable files, with scripts for reproducing the calibration. The body mesh is derived from MakeHuman reference anatomy. Automated checks cover saved flights, mission settings, injury timing and routine-search behavior.

We considered readability, performance and access throughout the implementation. The interface includes keyboard controls, reduced-motion support and a 2D fallback when 3D rendering is unavailable. Optional measurements and fictional starter profiles make the tool usable without access to private astronaut records. The current model uses group-level evidence and documented assumptions; baseline inputs scale the displayed measurements, and personalized medical use would require further validation.

AstroTwin's intended impact is to make NASA space-health research easier to explore and build on. It gives students, researchers and people interested in mission planning a practical way to connect a published measurement with an anatomical region, a mission scenario and a comparison they can inspect. Future work would expand the evidence base, test the model against independent human data and support more detailed physiological responses.
